claim: Severe forms of α-thalassaemia, haemoglobin H disease and haemoglobin Bart's hydrops fetalis, are an important public health concern in Southeast Asia.
source: Severe forms of α-thalassaemia, haemoglobin H disease and haemoglobin Bart's hydrops fetalis, are an important public health concern in Southeast Asia.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a general assertion about the public health significance of these conditions in the region.

claim: Information on the prevalence, genetic diversity and health burden of α-thalassaemia in Southeast Asia remains limited.
source: Yet information on the prevalence, genetic diversity and health burden of α-thalassaemia in the region remains limited.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in current knowledge in the abstract.

claim: 3595 (95% credible interval 1,717–6,199) newborns will be born with severe α-thalassaemia in Thailand in 2020.
source: We estimate that 3595 (95% credible interval 1,717–6,199) newborns will be born with severe α-thalassaemia in Thailand in 2020, which is considerably higher than previous estimates.
evidence: This estimate is derived from the geostatistical modeling and demographic data analysis presented in the study.

claim: The estimate of 3595 newborns with severe α-thalassaemia in Thailand in 2020 is considerably higher than previous estimates.
source: We estimate that 3595 (95% credible interval 1,717–6,199) newborns will be born with severe α-thalassaemia in Thailand in 2020, which is considerably higher than previous estimates.
evidence: This comparison is made explicitly in the abstract and supported by comparison with Modell and Darlison estimates in the results.

claim: Up to 5% of the world's population carries at least one α-thalassaemia variant.
source: It is estimated that up to 5% of the world's population carries at least one α-thalassaemia variant, with some populations (e.g. in India and Papua New Guinea) reporting gene frequencies of close to 80% (Piel and Weatherall, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Piel and Weatherall, 2014.

claim: Some populations in India and Papua New Guinea report α-thalassaemia gene frequencies of close to 80%.
source: It is estimated that up to 5% of the world's population carries at least one α-thalassaemia variant, with some populations (e.g. in India and Papua New Guinea) reporting gene frequencies of close to 80% (Piel and Weatherall, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Piel and Weatherall, 2014.

claim: Malaria protection afforded by α-thalassaemia mutations has been favoured by natural selection in populations with historically high rates of malaria.
source: Central to its elevated frequency is the malaria protection afforded by the underlying genetic mutations, which have been favoured by natural selection in populations with historically high rates of malaria (Flint et al., 1998; Premawardhena et al., 2017; Weatherall and Clegg, 2001a; May et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to studies on malaria protection and natural selection.

claim: α-thalassaemia is now common in other parts of the world due to recent population migrations.
source: Due to recent population migrations, α-thalassaemia is now common in other parts of the world, as illustrated by the inclusion of haemoglobin H (HbH) disease (a form of α-thalassaemia) in the newborn screening programme in California (Vichinsky, 2013; Hoppe, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations and the example of California's newborn screening program.

claim: Humans typically possess four copies of the α-globin gene.
source: Humans typically possess four copies of the α-globin gene.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about human genetics.

claim: In α-thalassaemia, at least one of the four α-globin gene copies is absent or dysfunctional.
source: In an individual with α-thalassaemia, at least one of these four copies is absent or dysfunctional.
evidence: This is a definitional statement about α-thalassaemia based on established knowledge.

claim: The severity of α-thalassaemia is inversely related to the number of functional copies of the α-globin gene.
source: The severity of α-thalassaemia is inversely related to the number of functional copies of the α-globin gene.
evidence: This is established medical knowledge about the genotype-phenotype relationship in α-thalassaemia.

claim: A deficit of three or more α-globin genes leads to the production of γ-globin tetramers (Hb Bart's) in the foetus or β-globin tetramers (HbH) in adults.
source: A deficit of three or more α-globin genes leads to the production of γ-globin tetramers, called Hb Bart's, in the foetus or β-globin tetramers, called HbH, in adults.
evidence: This is established medical knowledge about the molecular consequences of severe α-thalassaemia.

claim: Hb Bart's and HbH tetramers are not capable of transporting oxygen efficiently due to their very high oxygen affinity.
source: Due to their very high oxygen affinity, neither tetramer is capable of transporting oxygen efficiently (Galanello and Cao, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Galanello and Cao, 2011.

claim: The instability of HbH leads to the production of inclusion bodies in red blood cells and a variable degree of haemolytic anaemia.
source: Furthermore, the instability of HbH leads to the production of inclusion bodies in red blood cells and a variable degree of haemolytic anaemia.
evidence: This is established medical knowledge about the pathophysiology of HbH disease.

claim: 121 α-globin gene mutations have been identified as of July 7, 2018.
source: To date, 121 α-globin gene mutations have been identified (HbVar, http://globin.bx.psu.edu, accessed 07 July 2018).
evidence: This is based on data from the HbVar database accessed on a specific date.

claim: Non-deletional α-thalassaemia variants are typically associated with more severe phenotypes than deletional variants.
source: While deletions constitute the vast majority of these α-thalassaemia variants, non-deletional variants are typically associated with more severe phenotypes (Chui et al., 2003; Fucharoen and Viprakasit, 2009; Lal et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to clinical studies.

claim: Considerable phenotypic variability is observed even amongst non-deletional α-thalassaemia variants.
source: However, even amongst non-deletional variants, considerable phenotypic variability is observed (Singer, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Singer, 2009.

claim: Co-inheritance of α-thalassaemia and β-thalassaemia often leads to a reduced imbalance between α-globin and β-globin chains, resulting in a milder thalassaemia phenotype.
source: Because the geographical distribution of β-thalassaemia largely overlaps with the distribution of α-thalassaemia, it is important to note that their co-inheritance often leads to a reduced imbalance between α-globin and β-globin chains, resulting in a milder thalassaemia phenotype (Weatherall et al., 1981; Wainscoat et al., 1983; Kan and Nathan, 1970; Law et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to clinical studies.

claim: α0-thalassaemia variants (e.g. --SEA, --THAI) are common in Southeast Asia.
source: From a clinical perspective, α-thalassaemia is mostly a burden in Southeast Asia where α0-thalassaemia variants (e.g. --SEA, --THAI) are common and result in HbH disease when inherited with α+-thalassaemia (e.g. -α3.7 or -α4.2) or αND-thalassaemia (e.g. Hb Constant Spring, or Hb CS, or Hb Paksé), or in Hb Bart's hydrops fetalis when inherited from both parents (Weatherall et al., 2006; Chui, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Weatherall et al., 2006 and Chui, 2005.

claim: α0-thalassaemia inherited with α+-thalassaemia or αND-thalassaemia results in HbH disease.
source: From a clinical perspective, α-thalassaemia is mostly a burden in Southeast Asia where α0-thalassaemia variants (e.g. --SEA, --THAI) are common and result in HbH disease when inherited with α+-thalassaemia (e.g. -α3.7 or -α4.2) or αND-thalassaemia (e.g. Hb Constant Spring, or Hb CS, or Hb Paksé), or in Hb Bart's hydrops fetalis when inherited from both parents (Weatherall et al., 2006; Chui, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Weatherall et al., 2006 and Chui, 2005.

claim: α0-thalassaemia inherited from both parents results in Hb Bart's hydrops fetalis.
source: From a clinical perspective, α-thalassaemia is mostly a burden in Southeast Asia where α0-thalassaemia variants (e.g. --SEA, --THAI) are common and result in HbH disease when inherited with α+-thalassaemia (e.g. -α3.7 or -α4.2) or αND-thalassaemia (e.g. Hb Constant Spring, or Hb CS, or Hb Paksé), or in Hb Bart's hydrops fetalis when inherited from both parents (Weatherall et al., 2006; Chui, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Weatherall et al., 2006 and Chui, 2005.

claim: Recent evidence suggests a spectrum of mild to severe forms of HbH disease, with the worst affected individuals requiring lifelong transfusion.
source: Previously, HbH disease was considered to be relatively benign; however, recent evidence suggests a spectrum of mild to severe forms of HbH disease, with the worst affected individuals requiring lifelong transfusion (Chui et al., 2003; Fucharoen and Viprakasit, 2009; Lal et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to clinical studies.

claim: Hb Bart's hydrops fetalis is almost always fatal in utero or soon after birth.
source: Hb Bart's hydrops fetalis, the most severe form of α-thalassaemia, associated with an absence of any functional α-globin genes, is almost always fatal in utero or soon after birth, although intrauterine interventions and perinatal intensive care can lead to survival (Songdej et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Songdej et al., 2017.

claim: Intrauterine interventions and perinatal intensive care can lead to survival in Hb Bart's hydrops fetalis.
source: Hb Bart's hydrops fetalis, the most severe form of α-thalassaemia, associated with an absence of any functional α-globin genes, is almost always fatal in utero or soon after birth, although intrauterine interventions and perinatal intensive care can lead to survival (Songdej et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Songdej et al., 2017.

claim: A comprehensive review of α-thalassaemia epidemiology for the whole Southeast Asian region has not been performed.
source: However, whilst several narrative reviews of the epidemiology of α-thalassaemia in Southeast Asian countries are available (Chui, 2005; Fucharoen and Winichagoon, 1987; Fucharoen and Winichagoon, 2011), a comprehensive review for the whole region has not been performed, making the current evidence-base patchy and incohesive.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in the literature.

claim: There is a substantial amount of α-thalassaemia data available only in local data sources that is not being accessed by the international community.
source: In addition, there appears to be a substantial amount of data that are available only in local data sources, which is not being accessed by the international community.
evidence: This is inferred from the authors' experience in identifying local Thai sources.

claim: Modell and Darlison's estimates represent the only source of information on the epidemiology of thalassaemias and other inherited haemoglobin disorders at national and regional levels.
source: Estimates of the number of newborns with severe forms of α-thalassaemia published by Modell and Darlison currently represent the only source of information on the epidemiology of thalassaemias and other inherited haemoglobin disorders at national and regional levels (Modell and Darlison, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Modell and Darlison, 2008.

claim: Various inconsistencies have been identified in Modell and Darlison's α-thalassaemia estimates.
source: However, various inconsistencies have been identified in these α-thalassaemia estimates (Piel and Weatherall, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Piel and Weatherall, 2014.

claim: Modell and Darlison's estimates do not include most of the surveys conducted in the genomic era.
source: Furthermore, they do not include most of the surveys conducted in the genomic era, which has allowed accurate diagnosis through DNA testing.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of previous estimates.

claim: Haemoglobinopathies often present remarkably heterogeneous geographical distributions.
source: Finally, haemoglobinopathies often present remarkably heterogeneous geographical distributions (Piel et al., 2013a; Piel et al., 2013b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Piel et al., 2013a and 2013b.

claim: The keyword searches yielded a total of 868 unique potential sources of data on α-thalassaemia prevalence and/or genetic diversity in 10 Southeast Asian countries.
source: Our keyword searches yielded a total of 868 unique potential sources of data on α-thalassaemia prevalence and/or genetic diversity in 10 Southeast Asian countries: Brunei Darussalam, Cambodia, Indonesia, Lao People's Democratic Republic, Malaysia, Myanmar, Philippines, Singapore, Thailand and Vietnam (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a direct report of the search results.

claim: 74 potential data sources were identified from local Thai journals.
source: A further 74 potential data sources were identified by one of the authors (SE) from local Thai journals and independently double-checked for inclusion into the study (CH).
evidence: This is a direct report of the local search results.

claim: 75 sources met the inclusion criteria and were included in the final database.
source: Of all these sources, 75 met our inclusion criteria and were included in the final database.
evidence: This is a direct report of the final database composition.

claim: Data were available for 106 individual population samples: 58 from the online literature search and 48 from the local literature.
source: Due to some sources reporting estimates for more than one population, data were available for 106 individual population samples: 58 from the online literature search and 48 from the local literature.
evidence: This is a direct report of the database composition.

claim: 46 surveys provided data on α-thalassaemia gene frequency alone.
source: Forty-six surveys provided data on α-thalassaemia gene frequency alone, two provided data only relating to genetic diversity and 58 provided data on both.
evidence: This is a direct report of the database composition.

claim: The total number of individuals sampled was 133,649.
source: The total number of individuals sampled was 133,649 (the population of the region is estimated to be 647,483,729 in 2017), with a mean sample size of 1261.
evidence: This is a direct report of the database composition.

claim: The mean sample size across surveys was 1261.
source: The total number of individuals sampled was 133,649 (the population of the region is estimated to be 647,483,729 in 2017), with a mean sample size of 1261.
evidence: This is a direct report of the database composition.

claim: Thailand had the highest number of surveys published in the international literature (excluding local searches).
source: The country for which the highest number of surveys was published in the international literature (i.e. excluding surveys obtained through local searches) was Thailand.
evidence: This is a direct report of the database analysis.

claim: No published surveys were identified for Brunei Darussalam or the Philippines.
source: No published surveys were identified for Brunei Darussalam or the Philippines.
evidence: This is a direct report of the database analysis.

claim: In Thailand, the northern and northeastern parts of the country contained >75% of all surveys.
source: Within countries, surveys predominated in certain areas. For instance, in Thailand, the northern and northeastern parts of the country contained >75% of all surveys.
evidence: This is a direct report of the spatial distribution analysis.

claim: Data for southern Thailand came exclusively from Thai journals (n = 4).
source: Data for southern Thailand came exclusively from Thai journals (n = 4) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a direct report of the data sources for southern Thailand.

claim: α0-thalassaemia was the most extensively studied form (n = 97).
source: α0-thalassaemia was the most extensively studied form (n = 97), followed by αND-thalassaemia (n = 49) and then α+-thalassaemia (n = 47).
evidence: This is a direct report of the database composition.

claim: The predicted allele frequency range for α0-thalassaemia in Thailand is 0.57–4.46%.
source: The maps for α0- and α+-thalassaemia indicate clear spatial heterogeneity in allele frequencies, with ranges of 0.57–4.46% and 2.43–15.03%, respectively (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This is derived from the geostatistical model predictions shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The predicted allele frequency range for α+-thalassaemia in Thailand is 2.43–15.03%.
source: The maps for α0- and α+-thalassaemia indicate clear spatial heterogeneity in allele frequencies, with ranges of 0.57–4.46% and 2.43–15.03%, respectively (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This is derived from the geostatistical model predictions shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Predicted allele frequencies of αND-thalassaemia in Thailand range between 1.57% and 1.65%.
source: Predicted allele frequencies of αND-thalassaemia range between 1.57% and 1.65% only.
evidence: This is derived from the geostatistical model predictions.

claim: The highest predicted α0-thalassaemia allele frequencies in Thailand are found in the northeast of the country, along a belt across most of the north, and in Chonburi and Rayong provinces in central Thailand.
source: The allele is also predicted at frequencies of up to 4% in the northeast of the country, along a belt across most of the north of the country and in Chonburi and Rayong provinces in central Thailand.
evidence: This is derived from the geostatistical model predictions shown in Figure 2A.

claim: α+-thalassaemia has its highest predicted allele frequencies across the whole of the north and northeastern zones of Thailand.
source: α+-thalassaemia has its highest predicted allele frequencies across the whole of the north and northeastern zones.
evidence: This is derived from the geostatistical model predictions shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The estimated number of Hb Bart's hydrops fetalis births in Thailand in 2020 is 423 (CI: 184–761).
source: We estimate that the number of Hb Bart's hydrops fetalis births in the country will be 423 (CI: 184–761) in 2020.
evidence: This is derived from pairing allele frequency predictions with demographic data.

claim: The estimated number of new cases of HbH disease in Thailand in 2020 is 3,172, including 2674 (CI: 1,296–4,491) deletional and 498 (CI: 237–947) non-deletional cases.
source: The number of new cases of HbH disease is estimated to be 3,172, including 2674 (CI: 1,296–4,491) deletional and 498 (CI: 237–947) non-deletional cases.
evidence: This is derived from pairing allele frequency predictions with demographic data.

claim: The highest absolute burden of hydrops fetalis in Thailand is predicted in Bangkok City (57 [CI: 13–151]).
source: The highest absolute burden of hydrops fetalis is predicted in Bangkok City (57 [CI: 13–151]) (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), with its high population density, and Udon Thani (23 [CI: 6–66]) in the northeastern zone, where some of the highest α0-thalassaemia allele frequencies are predicted.
evidence: This is derived from pairing allele frequency predictions with demographic data.

claim: Modell and Darlison estimated 1017 births to be affected by Hb Bart's hydrops fetalis in Thailand in 2003.
source: Modell and Darlison estimated 1017 and 2515 births to be affected by Hb Bart's hydrops fetalis and HbH disease, respectively, in 2003.
evidence: This is a citation of previous estimates for comparison.

claim: Modell and Darlison estimated 2515 births to be affected by HbH disease in Thailand in 2003.
source: Modell and Darlison estimated 1017 and 2515 births to be affected by Hb Bart's hydrops fetalis and HbH disease, respectively, in 2003.
evidence: This is a citation of previous estimates for comparison.

claim: Using 2003 population data, the study estimates 709 newborns will be born with Hb Bart's hydrops fetalis in Thailand.
source: Using population data from the same year paired with our model-based maps, and assuming no consanguinity, we estimate 709 and 5469 newborns to be born with Hb Bart's hydrops fetalis and HbH disease in the country.
evidence: This is derived from applying the model to 2003 demographic data for comparison with previous estimates.

claim: Using 2003 population data, the study estimates 5469 newborns will be born with HbH disease in Thailand.
source: Using population data from the same year paired with our model-based maps, and assuming no consanguinity, we estimate 709 and 5469 newborns to be born with Hb Bart's hydrops fetalis and HbH disease in the country.
evidence: This is derived from applying the model to 2003 demographic data for comparison with previous estimates.

claim: The study's estimates suggest that the burden of HbH disease in Thailand may have previously been underestimated.
source: Our estimates are therefore consistent with those by Modell and Darlison for Hb Bart's hydrops fetalis. However, they suggest that the burden of HbH disease in Thailand may have previously been underestimated.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison between the study's estimates and previous estimates.

claim: 15% of the 5469 neonatal HbH disease cases in 2003 were of non-deletional types.
source: Moreover, whilst Modell and Darlison did not estimate the burden of non-deletional forms of HbH disease, our estimates suggest that 15% of the 5469 neonatal cases were of non-deletional types, which are usually associated with more severe phenotypes.
evidence: This is derived from the study's calculations.

claim: Among surveys testing for all three forms of α-thalassaemia, the overall α-thalassaemia gene frequency ranged from 0% in populations from peninsular Malaysia to 35.4% in Preah Vihar, Cambodia.
source: In our database for all of Southeast Asia, the number of surveys that tested for all three forms of α-thalassaemia was 40. Amongst these, the overall α-thalassaemia gene frequency ranged from 0% in populations from peninsular Malaysia to 35.4% in Preah Vihar, Cambodia (Munkongdee et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a direct report of the database analysis with a citation.

claim: A higher allele frequency of 49% was reported in the So ethnic group from Khammouane Province in Lao PDR, although the sample size was small (n = 50).
source: A higher allele frequency of 49% was also reported in the So ethnic group from Khammouane Province in Lao PDR, although the sample size for this study was small (n = 50) (Sengchanh et al., 2005).
evidence: This is a direct report of a specific survey result with a citation.

claim: The highest α+-thalassaemia allele frequency observed in the region was 26% in Cambodia.
source: α+-thalassaemia, the most prevalent form, reached allele frequencies of 26% in Cambodia (Figure 1B, Figure 1—source data 2) (Munkongdee et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a direct report of the database analysis with a citation and reference to Figure 1B.

claim: The surveys revealed a clear north-to-south decline in the distribution of α+-thalassaemia across Southeast Asia.
source: The surveys revealed a clear north-to-south decline in the distribution of α+-thalassaemia across the region, with a single high allele frequency estimate of 16.8% observed in Sabah in Malaysian Borneo (Tan et al., 2010).
evidence: This is inferred from the spatial pattern of survey results shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The observed allele frequency of αND-thalassaemia ranged between 0% in various locations across Malaysia and 16.25% in central Peninsular Malaysia.
source: The observed allele frequency of αND-thalassaemia ranged between 0% in various locations across Malaysia and 16.25% in central Peninsular Malaysia (Figure 1C, Figure 1—source data 3).
evidence: This is a direct report of the database analysis with reference to Figure 1C.

claim: --SEA was the dominant α0-thalassaemia mutation throughout the region.
source: Throughout the region, --SEA was the dominant α0-thalassaemia mutation, and in the majority of surveys -α3.7 was the dominant α+-thalassaemia and Hb CS the dominant αND-thalassaemia mutation.
evidence: This is inferred from the genetic diversity data shown in Figures 4-6.

claim: In the majority of surveys, -α3.7 was the dominant α+-thalassaemia mutation.
source: Throughout the region, --SEA was the dominant α0-thalassaemia mutation, and in the majority of surveys -α3.7 was the dominant α+-thalassaemia and Hb CS the dominant αND-thalassaemia mutation.
evidence: This is inferred from the genetic diversity data shown in Figures 4-6.

claim: In the majority of surveys, Hb CS was the dominant αND-thalassaemia mutation.
source: Throughout the region, --SEA was the dominant α0-thalassaemia mutation, and in the majority of surveys -α3.7 was the dominant α+-thalassaemia and Hb CS the dominant αND-thalassaemia mutation.
evidence: This is inferred from the genetic diversity data shown in Figures 4-6.

claim: The -(α)20.5 and --MED mutations were not detected in any of the surveys.
source: The -(α)20.5 and --MED mutations were not detected in any of the surveys, whilst the --FIL mutation was found in 2 of the 16 surveys in which it was tested for and --THAI in 9 of the 31 surveys in which it was included.
evidence: This is a direct report of the genetic diversity analysis.

claim: The --FIL mutation was found in 2 of the 16 surveys in which it was tested for.
source: The -(α)20.5 and --MED mutations were not detected in any of the surveys, whilst the --FIL mutation was found in 2 of the 16 surveys in which it was tested for and --THAI in 9 of the 31 surveys in which it was included.
evidence: This is a direct report of the genetic diversity analysis.

claim: The --THAI mutation was found in 9 of the 31 surveys in which it was included.
source: The -(α)20.5 and --MED mutations were not detected in any of the surveys, whilst the --FIL mutation was found in 2 of the 16 surveys in which it was tested for and --THAI in 9 of the 31 surveys in which it was included.
evidence: This is a direct report of the genetic diversity analysis.

claim: The model-based maps for Thailand are the first spatially continuous maps of the distribution of α-thalassaemia in any country.
source: The model-based maps for Thailand presented here are, to our knowledge, the first spatially continuous maps of the distribution of α-thalassaemia in any country.
evidence: This is stated as a novel contribution of the study.

claim: The newborn estimates represent the first evidence-based estimates of specific forms of α-thalassaemia disease amongst newborns since 2003.
source: Our newborn estimates represent the first evidence-based estimates of specific forms of α-thalassaemia disease amongst newborns since 2003 (although the study in which they were reported was published in 2008) (Modell and Darlison, 2008) and the first estimates at sub-national level.
evidence: This is stated as a novel contribution of the study.

claim: The estimate of Hb Bart's hydrops fetalis births represents more than 10% of the 3697 stillbirths estimated for Thailand in 2015.
source: Importantly, whilst there are currently no estimates of the number of stillbirths that will occur in Thailand in 2020, our estimate of the number of Hb Bart's hydrops fetalis births represents more than 10% of the 3697 stillbirths estimated for 2015 (Blencowe et al., 2016).
evidence: This is calculated from the study's estimates and cited stillbirth data.

claim: The newborn calculations in the present study represent a methodological advance over previous efforts to assess the burden of α-thalassaemia.
source: As such, the newborn calculations in the present study represent a methodological advance over previous efforts to assess the burden of α-thalassaemia.
evidence: This is stated as a contribution of the study based on the use of fine-scale data and geostatistical methods.

claim: The descriptive maps represent the first detailed cartographic representations of α-thalassaemia allele frequency estimates in Southeast Asia that take into account the specific geographical location of the surveys.
source: Our descriptive maps represent the first detailed cartographic representations of α-thalassaemia allele frequency estimates in Southeast Asia, which take into account the specific geographical location of the surveys in which they were observed.
evidence: This is stated as a novel contribution of the study.

claim: The maps demonstrate a severe lack of data on the allele frequency of α-thalassaemia across large parts of Southeast Asia, including Myanmar, northern Lao PDR, northern Vietnam, Indonesia, Philippines and Brunei.
source: However, our maps also demonstrate a severe lack of data on the allele frequency of α-thalassaemia across large parts of Southeast Asia, including in Myanmar, northern Lao PDR, northern Vietnam, Indonesia, Philippines and Brunei.
evidence: This is inferred from the spatial distribution of surveys shown in the figures.

claim: High variant heterogeneity has been observed for G6PD deficiency in Southeast Asia.
source: However, high variant heterogeneity has been observed for other genetic disorders (e.g. G6PD deficiency) in Southeast Asia, (Howes et al., 2013) which might suggest a similar underlying cause.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Howes et al., 2013.

claim: P. falciparum has been shown to display genetically structured populations within Thailand alone.
source: Indeed, P. falciparum has been shown to display genetically structured populations within Thailand alone. (Pumpaibool et al., 2009)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Pumpaibool et al., 2009.

claim: The evolutionary dynamics between P. falciparum and haemoglobin variants, including α-thalassaemia, may be more complex than currently appreciated.
source: It is possible that the evolutionary dynamics between P. falciparum and haemoglobin variants, including α-thalassaemia, are more complex than we currently appreciate.
evidence: This is stated as a speculative interpretation of the observed genetic diversity patterns.

claim: Areas with the highest proportions of co-occurring severe α-thalassaemia forms may experience a higher prevalence of the severe non-deletional form of HbH disease.
source: Areas with the highest proportions of co-occurring severe α-thalassaemia forms (i.e. α0-thalassaemia and αND-thalassaemia) may experience a higher prevalence of the severe non-deletional form of HbH disease.
evidence: This is inferred from the genetic diversity patterns and knowledge of disease severity.

claim: The predominance of Hb CS in surveys from Malaysia and Vietnam suggests that the health burden of α-thalassaemia in these areas may be greater than previously thought.
source: Furthermore, the predominance of Hb CS in surveys from Malaysia and Vietnam suggests that the health burden of α-thalassaemia in these areas may be greater than previously thought.
evidence: This is inferred from the genetic diversity data and knowledge that Hb CS causes more severe phenotypes.

claim: Hb CS is a mutation at the termination codon of the α2-globin gene, which in a normal individual accounts for three-quarters of overall α-globin production.
source: Hb CS is a mutation at the termination codon of the α2-globin gene, which, in a normal individual, accounts for three-quarters of overall α-globin production (Liebhaber and Kan, 1981; Orkin et al., 1981).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Liebhaber and Kan, 1981 and Orkin et al., 1981.

claim: α2-globin gene mutations, such as Hb CS, tend to cause a more severe phenotype.
source: As a result, α2-globin gene mutations, such as Hb CS, tend to cause a more severe phenotype (Chui, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Chui, 2005.

claim: The average mean absolute error of the predictions is 0.93%, 4.10% and 2.30%, for α0-, α+- and αND-thalassaemia, respectively.
source: The results of the 10-fold cross-validation procedure reveal an average mean absolute error of the predictions of 0.93%, 4.10% and 2.30%, for α0-, α+- and αND-thalassaemia, respectively.
evidence: This is derived from the model validation procedure.

claim: The average correlation between the observed and predicted values is 0.74 (0.62–0.83), 0.71 (0.49–0.85) and 0.47 (0.17–0.69) for α0-, α+- and αND-thalassaemia, respectively.
source: The average correlation between the observed and predicted values is 0.74 (0.62–0.83), 0.71 (0.49–0.85) and 0.47 (0.17–0.69), respectively.
evidence: This is derived from the model validation procedure.

claim: Country reports from Malaysia indicate a shift in the age distribution of thalassaemia patients towards older ages.
source: Moreover, country reports (e.g. from Malaysia) indicate a shift in the age distribution of thalassaemia patients towards older ages (Ibrahim, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Ibrahim, 2012.

claim: Substantial additional survey data can be identified in locally published sources.
source: Nevertheless, we have demonstrated that substantial additional survey data can be identified in locally published sources and, as a result, highlighted the enormous value of future collaborations to collate local data in other regions.
evidence: This is inferred from the study's experience in identifying 48 surveys from local Thai sources.

claim: Extensive variation in allele frequencies between different ethnic groups in similar geographic locations has been observed in Thailand.
source: Although extensive variation in allele frequencies between different ethnic groups in similar geographic locations has been observed in Thailand (Kulaphisit et al., 2017) and other countries (e.g. Sri Lanka), this could not be reflected in our predicted allele frequencies.

claim: Allele frequencies of around 3.65% for the Hb CS mutation have been reported in the Khmer ethnic group in Surin and Buriram provinces.
source: For example, allele frequencies of around 3.65% for the Hb CS mutation have been reported in the Khmer ethnic group in Surin and Buriram provinces, whilst our model predicts maximum allele frequencies of 1.65% here.
evidence: This is stated as an example of ethnic variation that the model cannot capture.

claim: Many studies have shown a positive epistatic interaction between α- and β-thalassaemia, whereby their co-inheritance results in the amelioration of the associated blood disorder.
source: Many studies have shown a positive epistatic interaction between α- and β-thalassaemia, whereby their co-inheritance results in the amelioration of the associated blood disorder (Fucharoen and Weatherall, 2012; Viprakasit et al., 2004).
